TEXT INPUT Feed it the output of `tree` (Unicode or ASCII box-drawing) saved to a file. Supported details: - optional root line: ".", "./", or a directory name (e.g. "src") - "├── name" / "└── name" entries; the indent width may be anything consistent (2, 4, 8 chars, tabs, ...) — depth comes from the marker column's rank, not from dividing the column index by 4 - a subtree pasted without its root line is handled (its top-level entries become direct children of the base directory) - trailing "/" marks a directory (as printed by `tree -F`) - `tree -F` suffixes (* @ = |) are stripped from names (--keep-suffix keeps them) - "# ..." comments and "N directories, M files" footers are ignored; names starting with "#" are treated as comments IMAGE INPUT A screenshot of such a listing is OCR'd (rapidocr-onnxruntime by default, pytesseract as fallback). OCR engines drop the box-drawing glyphs, so the "├──"/"└──" markers are located in the pixels themselves (their dash runs) and each name's depth comes from its marker's column rank; the OCR text column is used as a fallback. Small or dark-mode screenshots are preprocessed automatically. DIRECTORY vs FILE An entry is a directory when: its name ends with "/", or it has children listed below it. Otherwise it is created as a file. A directory that has no children listed (an empty directory) is indistinguishable from a file in `tree` output — that is the only remaining ambiguous case. By default such entries become files; pass --assume-dir to make them directories.
